newsitem.title: USA: COTTON--USDA estimate seen at 17.5-18.2 mln bales.
newsitem.headline: COTTON--USDA estimate seen at 17.5-18.2 mln bales.

text.p: After two consecutive crop estimates that shocked the market and bullied prices, industry sources are reluctant to stray too far from U.S. Department of Agriculture's previous prediction.
They pegged the output estimate between 17.5 million and 18.2 million 480-lb bales, compared with a forecast of 17.9 million bales USDA issued in September.
USDA will release its data Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
"I'm not a chicken, but I'm putting the estimate at 17.899, almost identical to where the USDA was last month," said Sharon Johnson, analyst with Frank Schneider and Co Inc.

Crop losses are likely to come in the Southeast U.S. where torrential rain contributed to plant rot. North Carolina, with record rainfall of 16.64 inches in the Raleigh/Durham area alone, could suffer the most acute losses, followed by South Carolina and parts of Mississippi and Louisiana, sources said.
Improvements are likely to show up in the Delta and Southwest, bringing the crop close to the USDA's September estimate, Johnson said.
Texas remains the wild card with the potential to produce a 4.0-million-bale crop compared to USDA's last estimate of 3.65 million bales.
"All in all, the September estimate was probably not bad," agreed O.A. Cleveland, cotton marketing specialist with Mississippi State University. Cleveland put the forecast at 17.5 million bales.

"This is going to be a very interesting number," said Carl Anderson, cotton marketing specialist with Texas A&M University. "I'm hearing mixed reports from the fields, and the bottom line is, I'm thankful for the USDA."
Anderson put the estimate at 17.7 million bales.
Other industry analysts said USDA over-estimated losses in its previous report as any damage is likely to result in losses of quality, not quantitiy.
"The USDA was a little too pessimistic on yields the last time, so I'll put my neck out and say 18.2," said David Brandon, vice president with Smith Barney.
He anticipates a stronger crop in the north Delta and California, and called Texas a wild card too.
Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes raised her output estimate to 18.1 million bales, with increases showing up in California, Texas and the Delta.

Besides production, imports will be one of the report's closely watched estimates. The deteriorating quality of U.S. cotton could keep foreign imports high, leading USDA to lift its forecast from 500,000 bales last month, sources said.
Imports for the week ended Sept 29 totaled 355,043 bales, according to the U.S. Census Bureau said.
"The (USDA's production) estimate doesn't take into account quality," said Ganes. "That is the key."
